Vigil

The direct answer to your question about how to format trapping data for analysis with Distance 7 can be found on the Distance email list all the way back to September of 2005 and I repeated that information in 2015

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distance-sampling/trapping$20web%7Csort:date/distance-sampling/YIrRB7GECME/9mrI9n0wEQAJ

"Each web is equivalent to a single point in a point transect design.  The sample effort is the number of trapping events.  Each trapped animal is equivalent to an observation in a point transect.  The distance of the trap
from the centre of the web is the distance to use for this "observation".

So, for example, say I had 1 stratum of area 100, containing 2 webs that I used for two trapping events (say trap nights).  I trapped 3 animals in the first (at distances 3, 5, 7) and 2 in the second (at distances 4, 5, 8) my
text file for data import might look like this:

area1 100 web1 2 3
area1 100 web1 2 5
area1 100 web1 2 7
area1 100 web2 2 4
area1 100 web2 2 5
area1 100 web2 2 8

Of course 2 webs is not enough to make reliable inferences about the stratum density, nor is 6 observations enough to reliably fit a detection function, but you get the idea. "

However, I would advise against this route for two reasons:

a) proper estimation of density from trapping web data relies upon guessing proper trap spacing; which is very difficult
b) estimation also depends upon capture probability at the centre of the web being 1 and diminishing thereafter.  With 31 traps, it is unlikely your design can conform to that assumption.  In my past (when I gathered data), I used 96-trap webs and was not able to produce data that could have reliable detection functions fitted; I suspect you would struggle with 1/3 that many traps.

Instead, I suggest you consider using "spatially-explicit capture recapture" (SECR) methods.  https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/SECR.html  However, even those methods are likely to require more sampling effort than you can produce with 31 traps.

Thanks,
Kevin

Hi Debra,

I'm a little confused about what each of the rows in your spreadsheet refer to. The rows with observations in them appear to refer to single observations, as they specify a single distance and cluster size. However, given that you have multiple (between 2 and 7) rows for each transect with no observations in them, I think these blank rows might refer to individual visits. So... did you never record multiple observations of pigs on one transect in a single visit? If you did, then summing the lengths of transects surveyed in column C isn't the right thing to do (observations made in the same visit shouldn't contribute length of transect multiple times to this total). Moreover you state that each transect was surveyed at least 4 times, but that some transects were visited more often. Transects K and O appear to have been surveyed 10 times each. Is that right? I think a nicer way of showing survey effort, rather than by including lots of line with blank entries, would have been to include a 'survey effort' column for total number of visits to each transect. You would then only need blank lines (one each) for transects where no pigs were seen on any survey (just three - F, G and P).

Assuming for the now that the total length of transect surveyed is correct, you surveyed a total of 46km of transect. The largest distance recorded by you is 50m, so we may consider that the total area surveyed by you is 46 * 0.1 (50m on each side) km. So, 4.6km2. In this area, you detected 62 pigs. You have stated that the whole study area is a little more than twice this large, so assuming that you detected all the pigs within 100m, you could assume there were around 130 pigs in total. Eyeballing the distribution of distances for these observations, I would estimate that overall detection rates were somewhere between 0.5 and 0.3. If we say 0.4, and divide 130 by this number, you get an overall number for the whole area of 325 - not so different from your own most recent estimate. So, these numbers look quite sensible, provided that you have specified survey effort correctly.

As for cluster size versus detection probability, it took me a while to understand this but I think I do now. I think this relationship will be used to adjust predicted densities calculated from the detection probability graph, in order to account for (very slightly) decreasing numbers of pigs per observation as distance from the observer increases (and detection probability goes down). So, when distance = 0 (and detection probability = 100%), the average cluster size is deemed to be 2 (i.e. log10 of around 0.3 from the graph). When distance = 50m (and detection probability is near zero), average cluster size is deemed to be around 1.5 (log10 of around 0.2). That seems vaguely sensible to me. However, someone with more experience in interpreting this graph may well be able to correct or improve this explanation!

Cheers,

Mark

messages.body_plain:
Debra

Mark has focused on what may be the central issue for you; have you described effort correctly such that Distance is properly accounting for survey effort.  His points regarding not having visit numbers enumerated in the data makes our interpretation more difficult.   It is also unusual to never have more than a single detection on a transect.  Recall also that for repeat visits of transects, the estimated density or abundance is an average across the time of the visits.

Now to your specific points.  (1) step back and note that the density estimates from all four of the fitted models are very similar.  The estimates of density are robust to the choice of model.  If your model fits the observed data, then you can carry on.

(2) size biased regression.  There is a video lecture and exercise that deals extensively with the issue of size bias in distance sampling.  You can view it at this URL

 <https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/#>https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/#bias-associated-with-group-size-estimation

Short summary of size bias: at low detection probabilities (i.e. large perpendicular distances) small groups are not detected, leading to bias in size of groups in the population.  This bias can be undone in several ways, one of which is to measure group size where detection probability is very high.  The graph you show is attempting to assess group size as a function of estimated detection probability.  The results for your boar data is that there is little size bias, and that average group size in the sample is an adequate estimate of average group size in the population.

(3) Precision.  CV is defined as SE(x-hat)/(x-hat)  namely the ratio of standard error of an estimate to the estimate itself.  That can be expressed either as a proportion (as I did in the formula I just wrote) or as a percentage (where this proportion is multiplied by 100).  In the current analysis, CV is expressed as a percentage (that's what Distance does), but the 2008 results you present, the CV is a proportion.  How do I know?  I take the SE(D-hat)/(D-hat)=0.243/0.65=0.3738.  To express this as a percentage (therefore comparable with the current analysis), you would have 37.4%

Precision measurements are also discussed in the online distance sampling course:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter2/#Measures-of-precision
Chapter 2 - Making distance sampling work <https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter2/#Measures-of-precision>
workshops.distancesampling.org <http://workshops.distancesampling.org>
In this chapter you will learn about the assumptions that underlie distance sampling. As density/abundance metrics produced by distance sampling are estimates, measures of uncertainty (or precision) need to be associated with them.Finally, a few suggestions regarding how a distance sampling analysis might be conducted: beginning, middle and conclusion.

Without knowing more about the 2008 survey, it is difficult to know whether the two sets of results are comparable. The general interpretation of density per unit area and study area size seem reasonable.  I suspect the reason for the two surveys is to determine if boar population size has changed in the 10 years.  I'll not perform a formal test, but my suspicion is that with a CV of ~40% for the first survey and a CV of ~20% in the current survey, even with the point estimates differing substantially, a formal test incorporating uncertainty is unlikely to show a dramatic (if any) difference.

(4) Nature of your detection distances.  One of the dangers of sending data to the Distance list is that somebody will play with it.  I did exactly that to see the distribution of the 40 detection distances.

On first look, the data look OK:

However, when splitting the data into smaller bins, the data look a bit less pretty; raising some concerns about field procedures:

The finer scale plot shows not quite half of the detections made at detection distance 0 (were surveys performed along trails cut in the jungle?) it also shows possible rounding to distances near 10m and 20m.  It is best for histograms (and detection functions) to have a shoulder (i.e. detectability should drop gradually for some distance near the transect).  That leads to better and more robust analysis.

messages.body_plain:
Bridget,

You are violating a critical assumption of distance sampling and without ancillary data you cannot correct for the problem. Ancillary data would be some data collected that can allow you to model how animals move in response to the observer before being detected. The other option is to modify your methods to reduce or eliminate this problem (e.g., make sure observers look ahead, especially on and near the transect line).

DISTANCE can still fit a detection function to your data but you have no idea how the violation of this assumption has affected your estimated detection probability. By judicious grouping of your data you can make it look like you are meeting the assumption but it really does not solve the problem because you don't know which detections occurred after the animal moved.

Another cause for such a distribution of detections is that the animals are not distributed uniformly with respect to distance from the transect (e.g., when roads are used as transects). There have been some methods developed to address this problem, but again they require additional data to model the non-random distribution of animals.

Regards,

Duane

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin, hi listfolk,

In general we don't have a solution for this as there are so many
variations on the theme (which summaries one might want) but hopefully
the below will help. It does assume a fair level of proficiency in R...

If you don't have any temporally varying covariates in your model,
you're done, there's nothing to average. (I realise this sounds obvious,
but just to cover all the cases.)

If you do have temporally varying variables in your model then you can
use the technique described in, e.g., Augustin et al (2009), Augustin et
al (2013) (in the former section 5.4 and 5.5, in the latter the appendix
has some (sparse) code) or even Marra et al (2011) section 4.4. A clear
example is given in section 7.2.7 of Wood (2017) (also in the 2006
edition but mine is not with me at the moment, I think around p. 249??).

The general principle is to generate posterior samples of the GAM
coefficients, then use them to generate new predictions. Sampling from
the posterior many times will allow you to capture the model uncertainty
in the GAM parameters. You can then make predictions for your time
periods and calculate the appropriate summary statistics (i.e.,
abundance for each day then average over the days) and store them. Those
values are then samples from the posterior of the "mean abundance"
statistic.

I uploaded some code at
https://gist.github.com/dill/1f601a4ad43a62cb327456f6bbbb49a4 which
shows how to do this for 2 time periods. In general you'd need to
include further "days" to this and it's much easier to concatenate all
the days into one big prediction data.frame and disaggregate the
estimates at the end (that's what all that subsetting is doing in the
for() loop).

Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave

PS. with apologies for whatever obvious error is in my code that you
find at a future date.

references:

Augustin, Nicole H., Monica Musio, Klaus von Wilpert, Edgar Kublin,
Simon N. Wood, and Martin Schumacher. “Modeling Spatiotemporal Forest
Health Monitoring Data.” Journal of the American Statistical Association
104, no. 487 (September 2009): 899–911.
https://doi.org/10.1198/jasa.2009.ap07058.

Lorance. “Space-Time Modelling of Blue Ling for Fisheries Stock

Hi Bridget,

To elaborate slightly on the points made by Duane: if you addressed this situation by grouping bins (say 0-120, 120-280, and then 2 more groups for the first graph; and 0-160, 160-280, and 2 more groups for the second) what you would effectively be assuming is that all animals that move away from your transect are still detected by you. The alternative is that at least some of these animals move away far enough that you only detect a proportion of them, or actively hide from you (so that regardless of the distance they move, they become much less detectable) before you have a chance to detect them. In this case, grouping to fix the pattern in your data could result in density estimates that are much too low. As Duane pointed out, here is also the possibility, if you are surveying in a landscape where habitat varies consistently with distance from your transect, that densities on the transect are lower than elsewhere.

You can see what an impact these different scenarios would have on estimated densities by playing with your data. Try supplementing your dataset with enough observations at and around zero to take your near bins up to levels that make a sensible looking detection function, and see what the estimates output from distance analysis on these supplemented data look like. You can contrast these with estimates based on your original data with grouped bins. The differences between these should emphasise how important it is to understand the distribution and movement of animals around your transects.

Cheers,

Mark

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] CPU performance
messages.body_plain:
Richard

I'm confused by the premise of your question because distance sampling is not a method associated with occupancy analysis.  Occupancy analysis estimates probability of occupancy, while distance sampling estimates animal abundance or density.

When performing design-based inference, covariates are used with the detection function.  It is seldom the case (with single platform analysis) that more than a couple of covariates are informative in the detection function.  Consequently, computing time for detection function fitting is quite small.

If you are performing model-based inference, using the density surface modelling engine, those analyses can be quite computationally intensive.  Distance does not use multiple cores for fitting an individual density surface model.

I'm not sure if that answers your question, if not, please respond off-list.

The short answer to your questions is that weighting of strata is not possible with the current version of ds() in the Distance package.  The default is for the "Total" to be equivalent to a pooled estimate in Distance for Windows.

You can prove this to yourself by using the "minke" dataset included in the Distance R package.  The identical data exist in the "Stratify Example.dst" sample project that ships with Distance for Windows.  The only challenge in proving this to yourself is that group sizes are associated with the Distance for Windows project, but the "minke" dataset treats each detection as a singleton. > Debra

> Mark has focused on what may be the central issue for you; have you described effort correctly such that Distance is properly accounting for survey effort.  His points regarding not having visit numbers enumerated in the data makes our interpretation more difficult.   It is also unusual to never have more than a single detection on a transect.  Recall also that for repeat visits of transects, the estimated density or abundance is an average across the time of the visits.
>
>
> Now to your specific points.  (1) step back and note that the density estimates from all four of the fitted models are very similar.  The estimates of density are robust to the choice of model.  If your model fits the observed data, then you can carry on.
>
>
> (2) size biased regression.  There is a video lecture and exercise that deals extensively with the issue of size bias in distance sampling.  You can view it at this URL
>
>  <https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/#>https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/#bias-associated-with-group-size-estimation
>
>
>
> Short summary of size bias: at low detection probabilities (i.e. large perpendicular distances) small groups are not detected, leading to bias in size of groups in the population.  This bias can be undone in several ways, one of which is to measure group size where detection probability is very high.  The graph you show is attempting to assess group size as a function of estimated detection probability.  The results for your boar data is that there is little size bias, and that average group size in the sample is an adequate estimate of average group size in the population.
>
>
> (3) Precision.  CV is defined as SE(x-hat)/(x-hat)  namely the ratio of standard error of an estimate to the estimate itself.  That can be expressed either as a proportion (as I did in the formula I just wrote) or as a percentage (where this proportion is multiplied by 100).  In the current analysis, CV is expressed as a percentage (that's what Distance does), but the 2008 results you present, the CV is a proportion.  How do I know?  I take the SE(D-hat)/(D-hat)=0.243/0.65=0.3738.  To express this as a percentage (therefore comparable with the current analysis), you would have 37.4%

Thanks to Eric for pointing out you are probably using the R package.

In this case, the process depends on if you are using the flatfile format (all data in a single table) or if you have a seperate table for each level of data (i.e. a region.table, a sample.table, a obs.table, and a dataframe with your observations).

For the latter, you can use something like this:

> subset.region.table <- region.table # make a copy of your region table
> subset.region.table $Area[subset.region.table $Region.Label != "MyStratum1" | subset.region.table $Region.Label != "MyStratum2"] <- 0 # Set the value of Area to 0 for all strata except your strata of interest, using an "or" operator to retain the area in more than one stratum. In this case, your abundance estimate will be the sum of MyStratum1 and MyStratum2.

If you are using a flatfile format, the idea would be the same, with slightly difference implementation. I don't have a code example, but it'll be very similar - find all instances of strata you want to use in the DF but not in the estimate, and set their Area values to 0.

Debra

When conducting point transects, effort is measured in terms of number of visits to the points (because the points have no length).  However, for line transects, effort is measured in terms of length.  That is why the "Survey Effort" field is of no use in your line transect survey.

To correctly record effort for transects that are of differing lengths and are visited differing numbers of times, use the product of the transect length and number of visits.  If transect 1 is of length 0.5 and is visited 4 times, effort for that transect is 2.0.  If transect 2 is of length 0.8 and is visited 6 times, effort is 4.8.

If there are 16 transects in the survey design, then 16 is the correct number of replicates.  With the elevated (incorrect) number of 120 replicates, precision of the estimates is underestimated.

Hi both,

I don't have a lot of experience at analysing transect data, so the terms in which I had been considering and writing about effort were from a thoroughly point-count based perspective. Apologies if that confused you, Debra. I wasn't even aware that the windows programme Distance makes no explicit use of a visit number field for effort in transect surveys - I was (it seems wrongly) assuming that the programme would take transect length and visit number for each transect and multiply them up itself. The few line transect surveys I have analysed with Distance in the past have had equal numbers of visits per transect, so visit number hasn't been terribly relevant (at for within survey comparisons). However, Eric's explanation that you need to provide Distance with the combination of visits and individual transect length, such that survey effort = total length surveyed, make sense, and accounts for why your survey effort variable wasn't affecting the output in Distance.

Sounds like you are just about good to go! Once you have correctly specified survey effort (as described by Eric), you can safely record all your observations on separate rows (each with the correct detection distance), because now rows are equivalent to observations (not to survey visits). As stated previously, the only situation in which you need to worry about including rows to account for a survey visit is when no animals were encountered during that visit - you appear to have done this correctly from the latest screenshots you attached. Something to note is that, in Distance, an alternative approach to accounting for visits where no animals were recorded is to routinely append a 'blank' row to your dataset of observations for EVERY transect included in your survey. For transects where no animals were seen, this will make sure that the survey effort on these transects is factored into density and abundance assessments. For transects with animal data, the inclusion of a blank row will make no difference. I don't think this approach would save you much time in this instance, but it can definitely be labour saving if carrying out separate distance analyses for each one of multiple species recorded during a point count or transect survey.

Cheers,

Mark

> > > > Short summary of size bias: at low detection probabilities (i.e. large perpendicular distances) small groups are not detected, leading to bias in size of groups in the population.  This bias can be undone in several ways, one of which is to measure group size where detection probability is very high.  The graph you show is attempting to assess group size as a function of estimated detection probability.  The results for your boar data is that there is little size bias, and that average group size in the sample is an adequate estimate of average group size in the population.

> > > > (3) Precision.  CV is defined as SE(x-hat)/(x-hat)  namely the ratio of standard error of an estimate to the estimate itself.  That can be expressed either as a proportion (as I did in the formula I just wrote) or as a percentage (where this proportion is multiplied by 100).  In the current analysis, CV is expressed as a percentage (that's what Distance does), but the 2008 results you present, the CV is a proportion.  How do I know? The few line transect surveys I have analysed with Distance in the past have had equal numbers of visits per transect, so visit number hasn't been terribly relevant (at for within survey comparisons). Something to note is that, in Distance, an alternative approach to accounting for visits where no animals were recorded is to routinely append a 'blank' row to your dataset of observations for EVERY transect included in your survey. For transects where no animals were seen, this will make sure that the survey effort on these transects is factored into density and abundance assessments. For transects with animal data, the inclusion of a blank row will make no difference. messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling in mountains
messages.body_plain:
José

Working in an heterogeneous habitat will present some challenges for your field methodology.  Have a look at these two resources:  Section 7.9.4 of Buckland et al (2001) dealing with "uneven terrain".  There is also a 2002 paper related to studying ungulates in rough terrain, found using the bibliography on our website http://distancesampling.org/dbib.html
@article{Peretal02b,
  author = {P{\'e}rez, J.M. and Serrano, E. and Alpizar-Jara, R. and Granados, J.E. and Soriguer, R.C.},
  title = {The potential of distance sampling methods to estimate abundance of mountain ungulates: Review of usefulness and limitations},
  journal = {Pirineos},
  year = {2002},
  volume = {157},
  pages = {15--23}
}

Detections made at extremely large distances from the transects (animals on ridge lines) are unlikely to help in fitting a detection function, as they contribute little information to describing how the detection is shaped in the region near the transect.  Inclusion of slope as a covariate is likely of limited value, because it is unclear how to define the location at which the slope measurement would be informative.  I can imagine a transect on the flat portion (slope=0) of a hanging valley, but an animal on a slope 500m from the transect.  What would be the recorded slope measurement?

You have the opportunity at the time you design your survey to define your study area; you might consider eliminating some regions as too topographically extreme to collect reasonable data safely.  It is universally the case that many shorter transects are preferable to few long transects for the purpose of adequately estimating encounter rate variance.  The balancing of a large number (20-30) of short transects, with the amount of transit time between transects (off effort) is part of the "art" of survey design.

On 26/09/2018 23:58, José Infante wrote:

> Hello,
>
> I have a query. For flat areas it is very intuitive that detection will decrease with distance very steadily, but what happens in irregular habitats?  if i do transects in valleys at mountain ranges, where i can easily spot large herbivores in top of hills, what is the correct approach? should i measure slope as a covariate? what if the valley's width is irregular or you can find cliffs (as those formed by river erosion) or hills that obstruct visibility to the rest of the valley? should i shorten the transect, fragmentate it or stratify?
>
> Thank you very much!!
>
> Regards,
>
> José.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance List,

We plan on developing new software to aid distance sampling practitioners in survey design and we would like you to help us make sure our software meets your needs.

Distance for Windows is currently the only software which provides practitioners with the tools to be able to design surveys and generate sets of randomised transects for carrying out distance sampling surveys. We now plan on making similar tools available in R, meaning it can be used on any platform. This software will allow you to define a survey design, e.g. equal spaced line transect design, assess the properties of the design as well as generate a set of transects for your survey.

We would appreciate it if you could take the time to answer the short questionaire provided in the link below, to ensure that we can best meet your needs.

https://standrews.eu.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_8A30qTNjVWNU5QV
